 can one mistake or one bad throw or one bad play rock your confidence? Hi, I'm Dr. Patrick Cohn with Brock McCormack. Yeah, one of the biggest problems with the YIPS is confidence can fade really quickly. Confidence in sports tends to be very fragile, especially after mistakes. Really with the YIPS, what happens is when you're focusing on failure and only looking at the bad throws that you make, you're going to exaggerate that and start to think that you don't make any good throws. Another issue and confidence killer is that when you find yourself comparing where you're at with where your teammates are at in terms of throwing. So we know based upon, you know, 30 years of working with athletes that confidence in general tends to be fragile for athletes. It doesn't make sense that you've executed thousands of plays literally or thousands of throws, and you have one or two bad plays or bad throws, and you're going to throw years of confidence building out the window. We call that fragile confidence. I'm only as good as my last play. Yeah, when I when I break it down with my athletes, I always say there's kind of two buckets of information that we can go to. And I asked them the simple question, where would you rather draw from to build your confidence? Well, that just gives a bigger picture idea that you know how to do this, right? So it's rebuilding the belief that I still know how to throw a baseball. I just need to build up the confidence and the trust to be able to unlock it again. You know, I always like to tell ball players, we're looking for nine out of 10. We're not looking for 10 out of 10. Let's not have that expectation that every single throw, every single play has to be there for you. Give yourself a little wiggle room. When you look into the past and think, oh, I used to be able to throw so well and I can't anymore, it's going to be hard to rebuild any confidence in yourself. So I always like to say to my athletes, we're creating a new normal, a new normal. It's not what you felt last year. This is new. It might be a little bit uncomfortable right now, but we got to create a new path forward and work with whatever we have right now because we can't get back the past. Are you feeling stuck and helpless with your throwing right now? Hi, I'm Dr. Patrick Conn. I'm here with Brock McCormack. We're here to give you some tips on how to get beyond the yips. You're watching the Sports Psychology Podcast. All right. So, what's the first step in really overcoming the yips? You know, many athletes feel overwhelmed and ashamed, you know, unsure of where even to start. Well, the first step is really acceptance. It's accepting that, hey, I have to make an adjustment now. There's something that's a little bit off between my mind and my body. Almost just accepting and leaning into the yips can make the experience a little bit easier because the more you try to run from it, it's going to get harder and harder to overcome. >> And I assume, Brock, when you say run from it, then players are actually denying what's going on with them and thinking that it couldn't be. They don't have the yips. They've seen their teammates have the yips before, but it's impossible for them to have the yips. And then what do they write it off as? Do they write it off as a bad day or do they write it off as a mechanical issue? Ultimately, if they're denying it, then what is it? >> Yeah, there's a lot of denial because people don't want to admit to having the gifts because there's a lot of stigma around how challenging overcoming this can be. And unfortunately, yeah, there are some bad stories about players dealing with the IPS. That doesn't mean it has to be you, right? So, the denial can get written off very easily as I'd say mechanicalbased issues would be the most common one I see with pitchers and catchers is something's off with my throwing motion. Well, the biggest problem is that players try to outwork the yips, which is if I throw more, if I work on my mechanics more, if I film my throwing sessions, if I get advice from a bunch of different coaches and teammates, I can outwork this problem. >> Yeah. And what's interesting, I think it's different for different people in terms of where it shows up. I mean, you and I have worked with ball players that it shows up in their short toss when they're just warming up. Maybe for a pitcher, they don't see it in the bullpen, but then once they get on the mound, they'll see it. So, it's across the board from just that short toss warming up with a teammate all the way to on the mound or on the field, it'll show up. So, what's the relevance behind that? Whether it's showing up in your practice and your short toss versus only when you get on the field. >> Well, yeah, that's an interesting phenomenon because it's not the same for every person. It's not oneizefits-all. So, I think the biggest step would just kind of be uncovering your triggers. Is understanding for you personally, when do these yipped up throws show up the most. Let's say if it is in those shorter warm-up throws, for example, well, you could mix in some specific drills like making athletic throws and throws on the run to start to build up your trust at the beginning of your throwing sessions. Well, let's say it only shows up during game situations. Then we have a little bit of a deeper problem we might have to get into there, which is worrying about fear. Fear of failure and fear of embarrassment that might be showing up in those situations. >> So regardless of where it shows up for ball players, the bottom line is they've got to get to a point where away from fear, away from over control, away from fear of embarrassment and get back to throwing how they're capable of throwing. So what's one or two steps that we can take to help ball players with this process so that they don't feel helpless? >> Yeah, I mean the first step is just kind of accepting it without any shame and realizing that just because you can't make these throws right now doesn't mean that you're not ever going to be able to make those throws again. You still have the muscle memory within you. It's just being covered up by a disconnection between your mind and your body. So, your mind is not allowing your body to move naturally. The first step is well, how do we rebuild confidence in being able to throw? Well, let's let's use baseball as an example. When you go to pick up a baseball, your brain is instantly going to go to, uh-oh, don't yip this. Don't overthrow this. So, a cool little trick you can try out is try to throw something else. You see a lot of MLB pitchers warming up by throwing a football. Well, a football and using a different object can actually re-trigger the brain to trust, hey, I can still throw. I know how to do this. And that can rebuild the belief. >> Yeah. You don't have any experience with that implement. I've seen PGA Tour pros, for example, they'll start chipping or putting with their driver because it's a brand new implement and they don't have any negative experiences with that implement. But beyond, you know, changing up what they're throwing, what else can they do to help them get back on track, feel like they're moving in the right direction? Remember, it's not an all ornone thing. It's not you either have the yips or you don't have the yips. What we find that some players there's some freedom of the throwing in certain situations and then in other situations where they don't have that freedom and we want to increase that over time. >> Yeah. Well, the biggest thing that pops up is over coaching, right? is over coaching yourself through the throw with too many thoughts. So our goal with our athletes from the jump is how can we simplify your thought process? Couple different ways to go about that. The first one is give yourself some couple cues to think about like hey trust and react. Commit to my target. Let it happen. Whatever verbal cues that you need to use to walk yourself through it can allow you to simplify the process so that you're not letting your brain continue to spiral. >> Yeah. and maybe even talking with a teammate while you're throwing to distract you from overthinking that throw. >> Yeah, a lot of a lot of interesting stories in overcoming the yips with distractions could be singing a song in your head, chewing gum, you know, there's a lot of different strategies, but all of those have the intention of shutting off the conscious part of your brain and letting the subconscious, the muscle memory shine through. So, bottom line here to help you see through the forest is to start in low pressure situations. Start to simplify your throwing. Give yourself some cues in order to help you rely more on your muscle memory or what we talk about is really motor memory. Simplicity in situations where you know you can build up that confidence with accurate throws. And then you build upon that. I've been talking with Brock McCormack. Hi, I'm Dr. Patrick Conn. === FILE: What Are the Throwing Yips？ ｜ Baseball Throwing Yips Tips [PQNErHCc_JE].en.txt ===

Have you ever been on the field and you can't make a routine throw that's been very automatic for you in the past? Hi, I'm Dr. Patrick Comb with Brock McCormack. We're going to talk about when a bad throw turns in to the yips and what's the difference between the two. You're watching the Sports Psychology Podcast. So Brock, when does a bad throw actually turn into the yips? What's the difference? Because I think some ball players, they can have a bad throw, it's not necessarily the yips or a couple bad throws, whereas the yips is totally different. >> Yeah. The biggest difference we see is that a couple bad throws or a bad practice doesn't necessarily mean you have to assume, oh, I have the yips. Everything's falling apart. The yips are pretty obvious when they present themselves in the sense of really spiking throws into the dirt or overthrowing your your throwing partner by a lot. It's confusing in that sense that you kind of experience just a sudden loss of motor control that usually happens under pressure. In these pressure moments, the stress, the fear, the overthinking, the playing to prove yourself, playing for earning playing time interrupt the muscle memory, causing the simple to feel impossible. >> Yeah. And it's just not the interruption of the muscle memory. Obviously, that's where we want ball players. We want them to trust in their muscle memory, what we call motor memory, because that's where memory resides in the brain, right? in the motor system, but coaches call it muscle memory. So, we go with that. It's the interference of what's getting in the way of that muscle memory. And often it's the overontrol and thinking too much about how to make a good throw for whatever reason. Maybe to get back on track or be as a coach says, try this. Then they start really overthinking it. And I think that overthinking comes from the fear of making another bad throw. Now, we're talking about the yip cycle, which we'll talk about in a later video. But there's definitely a process here when you have the yips is severe over control due to fear and then that loss of motor control. It's really because you're trying so hard to gain motor control. So, it's a little bit bizarre from that perspective. You're trying so hard to gain motor control that you're actually confusing your mind and your body and you're losing that control and that accuracy. >> Yeah. And one of the biggest misconceptions with the yips is that it's an end all beall. Like, oh, I got the IPS, it's over. Well, no. We're here to help with that. It's a temporary roadblock. It doesn't have to be the end. So, all it is really at the simplest form is a disconnection between your mind and your body. Your body still knows how to make that throw automatically. You haven't lost the ability to learn how to throw. Your mind just doesn't trust your body to be able to do it naturally. That's what we work on rebuilding is the trust. Well, I like to say fear is the opposite of trust. So, if we can rebuild the trust, the fear will start to diminish. Well, where does the fear come from? Well, two big positions that it comes from is the fear of failure and the fear of embarrassment. Well, if we think about where the YIPS pops up a lot of the time is in high pressure social environments. You get to a new school, you're playing for a new team, you're playing in front of scouts, you want to play to impress. Well, if you make a bad throw, our brain gets stuck in the cycle of fear of embarrassment and not wanting to do that again. >> Yeah. Or I could take the opposite and say not so much the fear of embarrassment, the fear of not being seen as the star, the fear of not making that starting squad, the fear of not getting to where you once were. A lot of times when ball players go from high school, they were the star and they get recruited in college and now they want to continue to have that star status. So, I think if you make a couple of bad throws, you walk a couple of batters, whatever it is, that can start the ball rolling in the negative direction, like I'm no longer have that star status that I desperately seek. >> Yeah. And that's a classic case of playing for others respect versus playing the game for yourself. Players that are really obsessed with others opinions around them and do a lot of mind readading, which we're going to break down in another episode, tend to experience the yips more because not only are they obsessed about what they're doing in their own mechanics, but then we call it the aftermath of the throw. Dr. Con, how do you explain the aftermath of the throw to your Yips athletes? >> Well, the aftermath is absolutely everything. It's not the fact that you made a bad throw to the pitcher. It's not the fact that you missed your throw down to second. It's not the fact that you walked a batter because you couldn't get the ball over the plate. It's ultimately what happens after that. What that means to you, walking a couple batters in a row, not having your command, what is that ultimately going to mean? What do you think that's going to mean to the coach, your teammates, and your position on the team? >> These are all very challenging issues to deal with. We're excited to guide you along this through this series. We thank you for tuning in. We have a well-rounded, battle tested program that we're going to walk you through, and we look forward to you tuning in. >> Yes. I get this question a lot from my MGCPs from athletes from parents, I look at mental toughness as really a catch-all phrase. A mental toughness is kind of like having a strong mental game overall if you have a strong mental game then you have a lot of positive qualities to your mindset essentially. So mental toughness really is the ability to number one take your practice game to competition consistently and obviously not choke in addition mental toughness is about being able to perform at the level that you're capable of in competition. So what are the mental skills that may be included under this umbrella of mental toughness? Well first of all you have to have confidence and what I mean by that is you have a stable level of confidence the confidence stays that a steady state and it doesn't go up and down depending upon what's happening during the competition or even in your warm-up. Secondly, you have a complete level of focus on the task at hand in other words you have the ability to immerse yourself into the moment and get into that zone that helps you perform your best. In addition to that you stay composed in other words when you make mistakes you don't flip out, get aggravated, get frustrated, or tank the game away for example. So mental toughness also includes that ability to make mistakes. Now there's another kind of hidden level of mental toughness I think that we need to talk about beyond the basic mental skills and that's being able to prepare yourself for adversity. We call it the ability to anticipate challenges and be able to cope with those challenges. So you can't really point your finger at what one thing is of mental toughness it's everything that we do in the mental game that makes athletes mentally tough from being confident, focused, trust in your skills, staying composed after mistakes, being able to deal with adversity, being able to communicate well with your teammates if you're on a team, being able to handle setbacks, being able to battle back when you're down in a game or in a match for example.
